source.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates SAE feature monosemanticity and redundancy in LLM representations and reports results that challenge the idea that SAE features form atomic, canonical units. It does not reproduce the toy-network method.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports reconstruction, sparsity, dead-feature, and other benchmark results. Those are not included unless they directly bear on feature monosemanticity, redundancy, or the SAE-unit claims. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures, across 600+ released and newly trained SAEs on LLM activations, whether SAE features meet monosemanticity and non-redundancy criteria (DAME by dominance quartile, decoder-cosine redundancy, a sharding case study, support geometry). It reports dominant features as less monosemantic and more redundant. This is direct evidence on V5, the claim that dictionary features are canonical atomic units. It does not compare SAE features with neurons or measure feature distribution across neurons, so V4 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the most dominant SAE features are systematically less monosemantic and more redundant, and that sparsity constraints may be met by polysemantic or sharded dominant features. They recommend dominance-stratified monosemanticity and decoder-similarity checks before SAE use. They also say the deficit varies by family and is not universal, and that larger-model checks do not establish scale invariance.
record.recipe_differences: This is an SAE evaluation framework and benchmark, not a toy-network superposition experiment. It uses DAME, decoder cosine similarity, and feature-support/context analyses across released and newly trained SAEs.
record.method_sensitivity: The DAME deficit varies by architecture and SAE family; Gated and JumpReLU are non-significant in the reported architecture-level test. The paper attributes some differences to L0 and hyperparameter transfer. Redundancy results depend on filtering dead-feature pairs and report robustness across decoder-cosine thresholds 0.1–0.9.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher sparsity (lower L0) correlates with higher dominance concentration across most architectures and families.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under stronger sparsity penalties, SAEs concentrate activation in a few dominant features rather than decomposing them further.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Track on Evaluations and Datasets
record.problems: Monosemanticity is assessed partly with an LLM judge and is a proxy whose score depends on concept granularity, evaluation data, explainer, and judge. The primary benchmark models are mostly 70M–2.7B; the larger-model checks cover limited combinations and do not establish broad scale invariance. Hyperparameter transfer creates large sparsity differences across architectures. The authors also note that their support geometry categories alone do not establish semantic sharding.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. General completeness, dead-feature, sparsity, and SAE benchmark results were omitted where they did not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Toy networks, the sparsity-dependent phase transition, and feature geometry are not studied.
The capacity-competition account of neuron polysemanticity is not studied.
Neuron polysemanticity without capacity pressure is not studied.
The study assumes LLM superposition and evaluates SAE quality. It reports no comparison of SAE features with neurons and no measure of features spread across neurons.
Stability across seeds and completeness of concept coverage. Completeness is proxied only by MSE, which is not reported per quartile and is not tested against a concept set.
Whether features are one-dimensional is not studied.

missing.what: Per-family DAME Q1 gaps, including GPT2-Small where Q1 outperforms Q2–Q4 (+2.7 pp) and OPT (+0.6 pp)
Larger-model DAME: share of SAEs with a Q1 deficit is 41.7% (Qwen3-8B), 50.0% (14B), 41.7% (32B) and 75.0% (Gemma-2-9B)
Binary AutoInterp on the same features fails to reproduce the Q1 gap (+0.13, +0.35 pp vs DAME -11.83, -9.50 pp)
Explainer-by-judge robustness: Q1 deficit from -3.25 to -18.84 pp across four cells. Frequency-matched deficit about -2 pp.
Absolute prevalence of redundancy: percentage of features with at least one redundant pair per quartile (Q1 0.19–3.81%)
Prevalence of sharding-compatible pairs: 2.6–3.8% of decoder-redundant pairs across L0 bins

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. I removed the V4 links from all rows: no row compares SAE features with neurons or tests whether LLMs contain recoverable sparse features. Monosemanticity evidence relies mainly on an LLM-judge proxy, and the authors state it does not test injectivity. Rows r9 and r10 use synthetic activations, not an LLM. The Gated and JumpReLU non-significant results were wrongly marked reversed; the authors attribute them to L0 above or near d_in. The redundancy states were changed from reversed to partial because only a small fraction of features is redundant, even though redundancy concentrates in Q1.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, overcomplete sparse features, their geometric arrangement, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated neuron dimensions while other features share them.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure. The study evaluates SAE features, not neuron polysemanticity or its causes.

The study evaluates SAE features on LLM activations, but does not establish that these are ground-truth features recovered from the model, quantify feature distribution across neurons, or show that all relevant features are recoverable.

The study evaluates monosemanticity and redundancy, but does not test feature stability across runs or demonstrate complete concept coverage. Its proxy metrics do not establish a definitive canonical feature set.
Whether underlying superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: All evaluated SAEs (per-SAE mean; 600+ SAEs)
rows.size_stated: SAE widths 4,000–128,000 features across the evaluated benchmark
rows.operation_detail: DAME token-based perfect ranking accuracy by dominance quantile
rows.uncertainty: Wilcoxon p = 6.76 × 10−8; Cohen’s d = −0.278; 65.2% of SAEs show a Q1 deficit
rows.note: The authors interpret lower held-out activation-ranking accuracy as lower monosemanticity among the most dominant features. This is an LLM-judge proxy, not a direct exhaustive test of concept-feature injectivity.
rows.check: Remove the V4 link. A Q1-vs-Q2–Q4 DAME contrast says nothing about whether LLMs contain SAE-recoverable sparse features. For V5 it is a modest, significant monosemanticity deficit (61.8% vs 64.1%), so partial.

rows.subject: Synthetic SAEs (105 total)
rows.operation_detail: Compare best-versus-second-best ground-truth concept correlation gaps by dominance quantile
rows.measure: SAEs with statistically significant Q1 deficit in monosemanticity gap
rows.value: 71 of 105 SAEs (68%) show a significant Q1 deficit (p < 0.05)
rows.note: The paper reports this as ground-truth corroboration of the dominance–monosemanticity relationship.
rows.check: Remove V4. These are synthetic activations with 128 ground-truth concepts, not an LLM. The row bears on V5 only as calibration of SAE recovery in a controlled setting; the subject should say so.

source_check.correct: The 105-SAE correlation-gap panel uses widths 256, 512, and 1024, with 128 ground-truth concepts. Widths 128, 192, and 768 belong to the additional 105 SAEs in the expanded 210-SAE containment panel. The reported 71/105 (68%) significant deficits are correct.

rows.subject: Synthetic SAEs (210 total)
rows.operation_detail: Measure prevalence-corrected held-out support containment by dominance quantile
rows.value: Q1 lower across 210 paired SAE-level contrasts; one-sided exact sign test p = 1.6×10−12
rows.check: Remove V4. Synthetic setting, not an LLM. The effect is small in absolute terms (about 0.01–0.024 containment).

rows.subject: All evaluated SAEs (per-SAE median)
rows.operation_detail: Count decoder-aligned redundant-edge endpoints by dominance quantile, with active-only filtering

conditions.value: remove pairs involving features with no observed firings

rows.measure: Q1 redundant-edge endpoint enrichment relative to active-feature share
rows.value: Median 1.64×; 71.5% of SAEs above the 1× null
rows.note: The finding is redundancy among high-dominance SAE features, contrary to the non-redundant-unit criterion.
rows.check: Remove V4. 'Reversed' overstates it: redundancy is concentrated in Q1, but only a small share of features are redundant (Table 15: 0.19–3.81% of Q1 features). So non-redundancy holds incompletely, which is partial.

rows.subject: All evaluated SAEs (per-SAE averages)
rows.operation_detail: Compare shares of within-quartile redundant pairs after filtering dead-feature pairs
rows.measure: Share of redundant pairs in each dominance quartile
rows.value: Q1 share ranges from 52–86% across architectures
rows.uncertainty: Overall Wilcoxon p = 2.2×10−57; 79.7% of SAEs have Q1 hosting the most redundant pairs
rows.note: Dead-feature filtering for the reported within-quartile shares removes pairs in Q4.
rows.check: Remove V4. This is a share of redundant pairs, not a rate of redundancy, and the filter removes only Q4 dead-feature pairs. Concentration is shown; overall prevalence is low. Partial, not reversed.

rows.subject: TopK-65k SAE on EleutherAI/pythia-160m-deduped
rows.operation_detail: Compare encoder and decoder directions and natural firing-support overlap for features 41902 and 46571

conditions.value: 192 held-out WikiText-103 validation texts, truncated to 128 tokens

rows.measure: Encoder cosine; decoder cosine; firings; co-firings; Jaccard support overlap
rows.value: Encoder cosine 0.2066; decoder cosine 0.7405; 316 versus 57 firings; 7 co-firings; Jaccard 0.019
rows.note: The authors describe these as two features with aligned decoder writes but dissimilar encoders and largely separated natural supports, a feature-sharding example.
rows.check: Remove V4. This is a single hand-picked pair: a counter-example, not a rate. Combine it with r14 as one case study.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, functional sharding example; Appendix J.9

rows.subject: TopK-65k SAE on EleutherAI/pythia-160m-deduped
rows.operation_detail: Independently add equal-L2 candidate decoder directions at positions where both native TopK gates are inactive
rows.measure: Change in target-token logit versus unmodified baseline
rows.value: Mean logit changes +0.556 and +0.611; 15/18 and 16/18 positive prompt-level effects
rows.uncertainty: Effect-vector cosine 0.943; candidate-pair advantage over matched controls +0.472 logit, bootstrap 95% CI [+0.347, +0.597]
rows.note: Both decoder writes increased the target-token logit in the actual downstream forward pass. This supports a shared-write/sharding interpretation, not a direct test of canonical feature completeness.
rows.check: Remove V4. Single-pair intervention that bypasses the native gates. It shows a shared downstream write, not prevalence.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, functional sharding example; Appendix J.9; Table 43

rows.subject: All audited decoder-aligned feature pairs (five SAE families)
rows.operation_detail: Classify natural activation-support geometry of decoder-aligned pairs

conditions.value: features each fire at least 20 times in pooled evaluation corpus

rows.baseline: Low-cosine matched controls: partition-like 80.0%, nested-like 1.2%, duplicate-like 2.1%, partial overlap 16.7%
rows.uncertainty: 95% CIs for full high-cosine pool: 17.6–25.6%, 11.5–19.3%, 25.1–34.9%, and 28.8–37.8%, respectively
rows.note: These support-shape categories are descriptive. The authors caution that partitioning also occurs among low-cosine controls and that sharding requires decoder alignment plus context-level evidence.
rows.check: Remove V4. The categories describe support shape only. Partition-like is more common among low-cosine controls (80%) than high-cosine pairs (21.5%), so partition-like alone does not indicate sharding. Duplicate-like at 29.9% vs 2.1% in controls is the clearer redundancy signal.

rows.subject: Audited decoder-aligned target pairs
rows.operation_detail: Blinded two-pass LLM audit of activation-context cards for stable sibling-subclass readings
rows.measure: Share judged to have a stable sibling reading; share with fresh support replication
rows.baseline: Low-cosine controls: 3.3% stable sibling reading; 3.3% fresh support
rows.uncertainty: Insufficient evidence for 51.4% of target cards
rows.note: The authors report these as descriptive audit percentages, not proof that all decoder-aligned pairs are shards.
rows.check: Remove V4. LLM-judge audit; 51.4% of cards had insufficient evidence. The uncertainty field holds the insufficient-evidence share, not an uncertainty estimate.

relationships.condition: Decoder-aligned feature pairs in evaluated LLM SAEs, especially high-dominance features
relationships.reason: Redundant decoder directions concentrate in Q1 (median 1.64× enrichment). Duplicate-like supports occur in 29.9% of aligned pairs vs 2.1% of controls. A functional sharding pair is shown. These contradict non-redundant canonical units (r11, r12, r13, r14, r15, r16).
relationships.display_finding: Redundant decoder directions concentrated among high-dominance features (Q1, median 1.64× enrichment), duplicate-like supports occurred in 29.9% of aligned pairs vs 2.1% of controls, and a functional sharding pair was shown.

relationships.condition: Monosemanticity of high-dominance SAE features (TopK, BatchTopK, Matryoshka, PAnneal, Standard ReLU; synthetic SAEs)
relationships.reason: Features remain partly interpretable overall, but Q1 features score lower. The deficit is 1.1–5.9 pp by architecture and 61.8% vs 64.1% overall. It is corroborated with ground truth in synthetic SAEs, so monosemanticity is not uniform (r1, r2, r5, r6, r7, r8, r9, r10).
relationships.display_finding: Features stayed partly interpretable, but high-dominance Q1 features scored 1.1–5.9 pp lower by architecture (61.8% versus 64.1% overall), a deficit confirmed against ground truth in synthetic SAEs.

tranche.reason: The study reports polysemanticity, redundancy and functional sharding that qualify or contradict treating SAE features as canonical explanatory units.

source_check.notes: Monosemanticity and decoder alignment are proxies; completeness, training-seed stability and canonical identification are not established. Table 45 uses SAE-averaged percentages, while Table 46 uses audited-card percentages.

statements.correction: Appendix J.11, Table 45: duplicate-like supports = 29.9% in the full eligible high-cosine pool; 27.4% in the matched high-cosine subset; 2.1% in matched low-cosine controls. Percentages are equal-weight means of within-SAE percentages. DAME measures explanation-based activation-ranking accuracy.
statements.problem: The support-geometry analysis is distinct from DAME's ranking assay. The comparison also leaves implicit that 29.9% describes the full aligned-pair pool, whereas 2.1% describes matched low-cosine controls.
